transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Um, I’m here because I’m having a really hard time staying on track at work. I’m a nurse, and on the floor there are just constant interruptions—an IV pump starts beeping, a call light goes off, someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or someone says my name—and it’s like whatever I was holding in my head just disappears.

It’s not just annoying; it’s becoming a real problem. I’ll be in the middle of thinking through a patient flow issue, or trying to organize what needs to happen next, and then one little interruption happens and I completely lose my train of thought. Then I’m standing there trying to reconstruct where I was, what I was supposed to do next, what I had just been prioritizing. It feels like my brain gets pulled off the track so easily, and getting back is really hard.

That’s the main reason I wanted to come in. It’s happening constantly, and in my job there’s always noise and alarms and people needing things, so I can’t really avoid it.

Do you find that your difficulty maintaining your train of thought happens mostly when there are interruptions or a lot going on around you, or does it also happen when you're in quiet, low-distraction settings like when you're at home reading or trying to plan something?

It’s definitely most obvious when I’m on the floor and there’s a lot happening around me. That’s the main reason I’m here, honestly. Like, I’ll be working through some kind of patient flow issue in my head—who needs what next, what I was about to do, what needs to be coordinated—and then an IV pump starts beeping, or a call light goes off, or even someone nearby asks another nurse a question, and suddenly it’s just gone.

It’s not even always that someone is talking directly to me. Sometimes it’s just my name being said somewhere, or a sound that pulls my attention for a second, and then when I try to go back to what I was thinking about, I can’t find it. I’m standing there trying to retrace my steps mentally, like, “Okay, what was I just doing? Which patient was I thinking about? What was the next thing?” And it happens constantly at work because there’s always something going off or someone needing something.

So yes, interruptions and a busy environment are a huge part of it. That’s where it becomes really noticeable and disruptive.

When you’re not in the busy hospital environment—like when you’re at home or in a quiet place—do you still find it hard to stay focused on tasks, follow through on plans, or keep your thoughts organized?

Yeah… I mean, it’s most dramatic at work, but even when I’m not in the middle of all the noise, I still have trouble organizing what I’m supposed to do and what order it needs to happen in.

Like when I’m charge nurse, especially, I try so hard to compensate. I’ll have little scraps of paper in my pockets, sticky notes stuck to whatever clipboard I’m using, half-started lists with patient rooms or things people asked me for, and then another list somewhere else because I couldn’t find the first one fast enough. It looks like I’m trying to be organized, but it doesn’t actually feel organized in my head.

The hard part is deciding what has to happen first. I can write things down, but then I look at all of it and I still can’t sort it into a clear sequence. So I end up reacting to whatever seems most urgent in the moment, or honestly whatever is loudest—whoever is asking me something right then, whatever problem is right in front of me. Then later I realize there were things I should have been tracking earlier, and I’m rushing at the end of the shift trying to catch up or tie everything together.

It’s really frustrating because I’m not ignoring things on purpose. I’m trying to hold the whole picture, but it turns into all these scattered pieces, and by the end I feel like I’ve been running around all day without ever really being ahead of anything.
Looking back, were you someone who had trouble staying focused or organizing tasks even when you were in school as a child, or did these difficulties only really start showing up later in adulthood?

No, it didn’t just start as an adult. Looking back, it was definitely there when I was a kid, even in elementary school. I did well in the sense that I was considered bright, so I think people kind of framed it as me being “careless” or “not applying myself,” but my teachers would write comments like that I lost worksheets, or forgot to turn in homework, or didn’t keep track of things.

And I remember my mom having to sit with me every night to keep me on task. Not because I couldn’t understand the work, but because I would drift off, or get stuck, or lose track of what I was supposed to be doing next. She’d basically have to keep redirecting me through the whole process. At the time it just felt normal, or like I was messy or irresponsible, but now when I think about it, it’s the same kind of pattern—needing a lot of external structure just to get through things.

Outside of work and school, do you find that these difficulties with staying focused or organizing tasks also affect other areas of your life, like your relationships, household responsibilities, or personal goals?

Yeah… it affects other parts of my life too, but honestly the place where it’s become the most concrete and scary is work. I know you asked outside of work and school, but that’s the part I keep circling back to because it’s not just me feeling disorganized anymore—it’s turned into something other people are formally tracking.

I’m on formal supervision now, and that’s been really hard to even say out loud. When I’m charge nurse, there are parts of my follow-through that other nurses have to double-check, because I’ll intend to circle back to something or coordinate something, and then it doesn’t happen cleanly unless someone else is watching the process too. And I hate that. I’m supposed to be the person helping organize the shift, helping other people keep the big picture, and instead I feel like people are having to compensate for me.

It makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader. That’s probably the thing that scares me most. I worked really hard to get to where I am, and I care a lot about doing things safely and being someone my coworkers can rely on. So having them need to double-check me, or knowing management is watching my follow-through formally, is just… humiliating and frightening. It makes me second-guess myself constantly.

Do you also find it hard to stay focused or keep things organized in your personal life—like managing household tasks, following through on plans with friends or family, or keeping track of personal responsibilities?

Yes. I wish I could say it’s only at work, but it’s not. At home it shows up in these really basic things that should be automatic, and somehow they just… fall out of my head.

Like I’ll need to call a family member back, and I really do mean to. I’ll see the missed call, think, “Okay, I’ll call after I finish this one thing,” and then it’s gone. And then two days later they’ll text again, or I’ll suddenly remember at some completely random time, and I feel awful because it looks like I don’t care. It’s not that I don’t care. I just don’t seem to hold onto the task unless it’s right in front of me.

Bills are another one. I can know a bill is due, I can even set a reminder, and then the reminder goes off at a bad time or I dismiss it thinking I’ll do it in ten minutes, and then I just… don’t. Same with appointments. I’ve missed or nearly missed things because I had the intention, I had maybe even written it down somewhere, but I didn’t actually get myself there or remember at the right moment.

And it’s embarrassing because these are normal adult things. It’s not complicated, it’s not like I don’t understand how to pay a bill or return a call. It’s the follow-through part. Even if I care about it, even if I make a note or set a reminder, it doesn’t always translate into me actually doing it when I’m supposed to.
When you were a child, did you have trouble staying focused or keeping things organized in settings outside of school, like at home or with friends?

Yeah, I mean… the clearest memories are still tied to school things, but they definitely spilled over at home too. Even in elementary school, it wasn’t just that I’d get a bad grade or something. Teachers would write that I was bright but careless, and there were constant comments about me losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework. And then at home, my mom was the one trying to manage the fallout of that every night.

She would have to sit with me and basically keep me moving through homework step by step. Not because I didn’t understand it — I usually did — but because if she walked away, I’d drift off or lose the worksheet or forget what I was supposed to be doing next. I remember her reminding me over and over, like, “Do the next problem,” or “Put that in your folder,” or “Don’t forget to bring this back tomorrow.” It felt like I needed someone external to hold the whole process together for me.

So yes, at home it was very much there. I think people just interpreted it as me being messy or not trying hard enough because I was bright enough that it didn’t look like a learning issue. But looking back, my mom had to provide a lot of structure just so I could get through basic school-related responsibilities outside the classroom.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of inattention, disorganization, and difficulty with task follow-through have been consistently present since childhood and significantly impair functioning in multiple domains (work, home, personal responsibilities), strongly supporting a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. Other candidates (F48.1, F06.81, F06.89) are less likely given the chronic and developmental nature of the symptoms and absence of predominant mood, psychotic, or other organic features.
